Virgin, Bride, Mother: Mary and Mystagogy in the Late Medieval Low Countries c.1250-c.1550

## Abstract

While the imitation of Christ has been abundantly explored in late medieval devotional

literature, and in mystical texts specifically, the imitation of his mother, the Virgin Mary, was also

a significant theme. This dissertation draws attention to the imitation of Mary as an important, yet

often overlooked, aspect of mystical texts, particularly vernacular mystical literature written in

Middle Dutch between c.1250-c.1550. Mary has often been defined by her inimitability—her

perfection as simultaneously a virgin, bride, and mother was definitionally inaccessible to earthly

women. Here, however, I argue that some vernacular mystical texts exhort the imitation of Mary

in and through these paradoxes, which they present as constitutive to the mystical encounter with

God. This imitation of Mary is particularly evident in what I have called mystagogical texts—

works that instruct, guide, and exhort their audience toward the mystical encounter. While mystical

texts in many genres could teach or instruct, the mystagogical function is particularly evident in

texts like sermons and liturgical commentaries that invoke or address their reader or audience

directly.

My analysis of such mystagogical texts, many of which have rarely been studied, takes

place across four chapters.  First, I explore Mary’s role as an underexplored aspect of the canonical

mystical authors Bernard of Clairvaux and Hadewijch. I argue that, while Bernard’s IV Homilies

in Praise of the Virgin Mother put forth a model of Mary as a paradoxical and inaccessible ideal,

the rhetorical strategies employed in the Homilies also enable later vernacular authors to present

Mary as an imitative figure. I show this first in the mystical writings of Hadewich, at the end of


<!-- Page 6 -->


iv

Chapter One. I then explore, in Chapters Two and Three, the imitation of Mary in the Limburg

Sermons, a collection of anonymous vernacular mystical sermons that draw on both Bernard and

Hadewijch. I argue that Mary is central to the sermons’ mystaogogy as virgin, bride, and mother.

The same is true for the texts I analyze in Chapter Four: the Evangelical Pearl, the Temple of Our

Soul, and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons. These sixteenth-century mystical texts, all by female

authors, portray Mary as an ideal contemplative, and invoke her example in their creative

expression of late medieval mystical topoi. Throughout the dissertation, I show how these

mystagogical texts sought to both teach and transform, presenting the Virgin Mary as the ideal

model for the mystical encounter and employing specific rhetorical and exegetical technique that,

in provoking a sense of immediacy and intimacy, assimilate their audiences (both male and female)

to her example.

## INTRODUCTION

Virgin, Bride, Mother

The opening paragraphs of an anonymous Middle Dutch mystical text known as Limburg

Sermon 39, or “This is the Book of the Orchard,” exhort its audience to “love God with burning

love.”1 They should not love in order to gain a reward, nor with a love that is lukewarm, but should

“love him like a mother her child, like a bride her bridegroom.”2 As the very first words of the text

make clear, the model for this burning love is the Virgin Mary: “May God greet us all, with the

angel Gabriel, by whom Mary was greeted when she was filled with the Holy Spirit.”3 As Virgin

Mother, Mary embodies—quite literally—the pinnacle of female perfection. Likewise, this text

suggests, she models the full spectrum of spiritual love—rapturous, hungry, self-displacing, but

also maternal, protective, and sacrificial. LS 39 not only claims that its audience can imitate Mary’s

love, it makes this claim by expressing a desire to be greeted or hailed as Mary at the moment of

her Annunciation. LS 39 likely originated as a letter, written sometime in the thirteenth century

from one religious woman to another, but was later adapted into a sermon manuscript owned by a

male semi-religious community. In another letter, likely written around the same time, the mystical

writer Hadewijch invokes a similar imitation of Mary’s Annunciation. She says, “Thus I begin

with the proper humility, with which his lover began, with which she drew him into her. One

should do the same, who wishes to draw God into himself, and enjoy him in love.”4 Here

Hadewijch herself channels Mary’s humility, but this is no modesty topos. Rather, Mary is figured

as the desirous lover (minnerse) of God, who attracted, even drew (trac) him to her. Mary’s

humility is yoked with this mystical love; Hadewijch channels her example and encourages her

audience to do the same.

This dissertation draws attention to the imitation of Mary as an important, yet often

overlooked, theme in mystical texts, particularly vernacular mystical literature written in Dutch

between c.1250-1550. The imitation of Christ has been, and continues to be, abundantly explored

as central within late medieval devotion more broadly, and within mystical texts specifically.

Christ, the God-man, was unique among human beings. Nonetheless, the first Christian thinkers

assigned fundamental theological significance not only to following Christ’s ethical teachings, but

to radically imitating him. Early converts and martyrs adopted Christ’s apostolic poverty and

virginity and his physical suffering and self-sacrifice, and sought, like him, to be filled with the

Holy Spirit. By the fourth century, Augustine, whose thinking was the scaffold undergirding

medieval theology, frequently urged the imitation of Christ as the central goal of Christian life.5

For more radical Christian mystical writers, the imitation of Christ could even lead to deification,

union between the soul and God so intimate that, as God had become man, man could become

God.6

However, the imitation of Mary has not been considered so self-evident. The history of

Mary has more often been told as one of veneration, adoration, and supplication, than of imitation.

As Christ’s humanity became more prominent in Christian literature, art, song, and ritual practice,

attention and devotion to his mother, from whom he received his humanity, and to the bond

between Christ and Mary also increased.7 On the one hand, these representations took for granted,

on some level, that Mary should be imitated, especially by women. Indeed, Mary was often more

closely connected to the construction of ideal womanhood than Christ to idealized manhood.8 For

this very reason, however, the imitation of Mary has often been considered an idealized and

asymptotic goal, the benchmark against which all women are measured and, inevitably, fall short.

Marina Warner’s feminist classic Alone of All Her Sex: The Myth and Cult of the Virgin Mary

(1976) laid bare the long history of Mary as the impossible standard of feminine perfection, even

as Warner also captures the awe, affection, comfort, and inspiration found in her “myth and cult.”9

Here, I propose that a group of late medieval, largely vernacular mystical texts illustrates

another way of thinking about Mary’s paradoxes, one that foregrounds her imitability as a model

for the most intimate encounter with and experience of God. I do not take one single text, author,

or genre as a point of departure. Rather, as I describe in more detail below, I draw on a variety of

sources, many of which have only rarely been treated in scholarship, to illustrate Mary’s exemplary

role. While many of the texts under consideration here are anonymous, Chapter One begins with

an analysis of two well-known authors: Bernard of Clairvaux (1090-1153) and Hadewijch (fl.

before 1250). Bernard’s IV Homilies in Praise of the Virgin Mother sets out the blueprint for the

hope to shed new light on both the figure of Mary and the study of mystical literature.

The Mystical Mary There is an enormous scholarly literature on both the Virgin Mary in the Middle Ages, and

on medieval (vernacular) mysticism. However, there has been relatively little attention paid to the

portrayal of Mary within mystical texts, or of Mary as a mystical contemplative. Stephen

Mossman, whose work on the Franciscan writer Marquard of Lindau (d.1392) is one of the

exceptions that proves this rule, writes that “Marquard stands at the zenith of a long medieval

tradition of presenting Mary as a mystical contemplative which, until now, has scarcely been

recognized as such.”10 Mossman traces the genesis of this aspect of Mary to two fundamental

aspects of Marian devotion. First, Mary became associated with the contemplative figure of Mary

Mary and mystical union was more often implied than explicitly stated or elaborated, and there

has been little major scholarly investigation of them, especially because these works did not

significantly inflect scholastic Mariology or the development of (and debates over) core elements

of Marian doctrine such as Mary’s perpetual virginity, her bodily assumption into heaven, and

(later) her Immaculate Conception.17

As a number of authors have suggested, this imagery of spiritual pregnancy and birth has

an uneasy relationship with the parturient and maternal experiences of women, historical and

contemporary. A question simmers, always, about whether these images of spiritual pregnancy

(and the figure of Mary writ large) help to provide a “discourse” for the enmeshment of self and

body that characterize pregnancy, motherhood, and care work, or whether they instead only reify

the subjugation of such entangled subjects.39 From the mid-twentieth-century on, medieval texts

have provided a trove of examples for theorists emerging from the psychoanalytic and feminist

this discourse without being subsumed by it, while reducing and essentializing women writers to

From Mysticism to Mystagogy This project further contributes to mysticism studies more broadly, first with its focus on

the seldom-studied theme of Mary, and second by centering what I broadly call mystagogical texts.

To attempt a definition of (Christian) “mysticism” or the term “mystical” is not my aim here,

particularly because none of the texts I consider here attempt to chart a comprehensive or cohesive

definition, summa or scheme for their mystical theology. When I discuss mystical texts, I have in

mind Bernard McGinn’s now canonical understanding of the mystical as that which is concerned

with “the preparation for, the consciousness of, and the reaction to what can be described as the

immediate or direct presence of God.”42 McGinn’s definition is helpful for this project not only

because it considers “mystical” to be a broad tent, but because it focuses on the encounter—the

word I choose more often than ‘“experience” in this project—with God rather than requiring this

CHAPTER ONE From ‘Blessed Among Women’ to ‘Mother of Love:’ Mary in the Writings of Bernard of Clairvaux and Hadewijch

## Introduction

If one of the primary purposes of this dissertation project is to shed new light on anonymous

mystical texts written in vernacular Middle Dutch, it may seem strange to begin its first chapter

with an analysis of sources in Latin, written by, perhaps, the best known and most ubiquitous

spiritual author of the Middle Ages. However, there is perhaps no individual figure who looms

larger in these texts’ discussions of mysticism, preaching and teaching, the Virgin Mary, and the

intersection of these themes than Bernard of Clairvaux (1090-1153). Because my sources so often

begin with Bernard, so will I. The literature on Bernard in relation to both mysticism and Mary is

vast, however, his early IV Homilies on the Blessed Virgin Mother, while often referenced, have

rarely been examined in depth. These four short sermons on Luke 1:26-127 (missus est angelus

Gabriel a Deo) form a comprehensive, yet compact summa of Marian devotion. While it has often

been argued that Bernard’s portrayal of the Virgin is not theologically innovative, and while the

sermons themselves are not mystical texts, they instill a relationship both to Mary and to spoken

language that proved influential for the mystical portrayal of the Virgin Mary in the Limburg

Sermons and other texts.

In this chapter, I will thus first, in Part 1, introduce the IV Homilies, and show how, in these

four short sermons, Bernard sets out the essential paradoxes that I will explore in greater detail in

the three subsequent chapters of this dissertation: Mary’s unique confluence of virginity, humility

and motherhood, the virtue of her silence combined with the impact of her speech, and her free

consent to Christ’s Incarnation with her complete obedience and conformity to God’s will. Bernard

exhorts his audience’s imitation of Mary’s virtues while simultaneously proclaiming the


<!-- Page 36 -->

more deconstructively, showing how, although Bernard emphasizes Mary’s singularity, both his

theology and his rhetoric set in motion an affective model for mystical engagement with Mary and

her speech that will be taken up by later authors. The sermon format, and the shifting target of its

second person address, creates perpetual slippage between the trio of Bernard, his imagined

audience, and the Virgin herself. These rhetorical tactics also introduce a set of theological

questions surrounding Mary’s will and consent as I explore in Part 3 through Bernard’s reading of

and 5, which turn from Bernard to the Middle Dutch mystical tradition, I provide a comparative

differs from his. Where Bernard emphasizes the threefold paradoxes of Mary’s virginity and

paradoxical qualities in a different combination. Hadewijch frames Mary’s humility in three ways

that markedly differ from Bernard’s. First, rather than emphasize Mary’s meekness or silence, she

Bernard, she also dwells on Mary’s pregnancy, presenting this embodied suffering as another

manifestation of Mary’s humility. Finally, Hadewijch, in emphasizing Mary’s motherhood over

and above her virginity, presents Mary not as an inimitable paragon, but as a mentor and guide to

the mystical life. Since I have explored Hadewijch’s Marian imagery in previous work, I will not

## CHAPTER TWO Teaching and Preaching Love: Mystagogy in the Limburg Sermons

## Introduction

The next two chapters examine the imitation of the Virgin Mary in the Limburg Sermons,

a mystical sermon collection written in vernacular Middle Dutch and compiled sometime around

1300. This unusual corpus of sermons, many of which are translated and adapted from an earlier

Middle High German collection known as the St. Georgen Sermons, provides a rich opportunity

to consider the sermon as a mystagogical tool.208 The sermons display a self-reflexive interest in

the process of preaching itself and the author(s), compiler(s), and audiences of the collection were

deeply familiar with mystical themes and vocabulary. Here I argue that they saw the sermon as a

vehicle not only for moral regulation or scriptural exegesis, but also for interior transformation,

eliciting as well as describing mystical encounters. Moreover, I argue that the Virgin Mary is

central as a model for the relationship between preaching and mysticism throughout the corpus.

The sermons exploit Mary’s potent metaphorical multivalency to cast her as the ideal mystical

subject, whom the sermons’ audience should strive to imitate.

In Chapter Two I first, in Part 1, provide an introduction to the Limburg Sermons, which

have not been translated, and which have received little attention in scholarship.209 In Part 2, I

show how the sermons thematize preaching itself, and present both the preached and written

sermon as sites of mystical encounter. In Parts 3 and 4 I draw out this argument for the sermons’

mystagogy with a close reading of two sermons—LS 16 and LS 45. I suggest that these sermons

Part 1. The Limburg Sermons and Manuscript H

The Limburg Sermons [Limburgsche sermoenen] refers to a collection of 48 sermons

written in vernacular Middle Dutch and compiled in a single manuscript currently housed in the

Royal Library of the Netherlands, The Hague Koninklijke Bibliotheek MS 70 E 5, known as MS

H.211 They are by far the oldest sermons found in the Dutch language, and some of its oldest

surviving religious prose. The identity of their author(s) and compiler(s) is unknown, but the

collection was evidently assembled with care. A detailed Table of Contents, the oldest example of

such a feature in Middle Dutch literature, proclaims: “Here, one finds all the sermons of this book.”

[Hier vint mi alle de sermone van den bueke].212 Yet while bound together in a handsome volume

and unified by this Table of Contents, the collection is heterogeneous. Thirty-two of the forty-eight

sermons are translations of an earlier thirteenth-century Middle High German sermon collection,

the Sankt-Georgener Predigten, or St. Georgen Sermons.213 The other sixteen sermons, however,

including some of the longer and more complex texts in the collection, cannot be traced to earlier

imaginatively incorporate the vested power of the sermon and the preaching act into their own

Conclusions I have shown here that the Limburg Sermons are interested in and committed to inciting

Part 4. Bride and Mother: The Virgin Mary in the Garden of Love The history of medieval Christian exegesis of the Song of Songs has typically been written

around the different types represented by the figure of the Bride. Allegorical interpretations of the

Song maintained a stable identification of the Bridegroom as God or Christ, but the identity of the

Bride could range widely and inventively, though she most often represented some combination

of the Church, the individual soul, or the Virgin Mary.417 The most significant developments in

this tradition involved, broadly speaking, what E. Ann Matter has called a move from allegorical

to tropological interpretation, that is, from a mode which, fundamentally historical, used the figures

of the Song to tell the story of Christ and the Church, to a mode fundamentally oriented towards

the present and future, in which the reader of the commentary was asked to place herself in the

role of the Bride and cultivate her own relationship with the heavenly Bridegroom. In twelfth-

century France, on the eve of the composition of the St. Georgen Sermons and the Limburg

Sermons, these tropological commentaries sometimes had a more mystical orientation, as in the

Conclusions I have focused here on two main aspects of this imitatio Mariae: the expansion of

expressions of Mary’s desire for the Incarnation through various rhetorical techniques that enable

her to speak as the powerful figure of Wisdom and as the Bride in the Song of Songs, and the use

of garden imagery, also drawn primarily from the Song, which likewise emphasizes Mary as a

model for desire and union as well as for chastity and humility. I have argued not only for the

imitation of Mary as a central hermeneutic within the mystagogy of the Limburg Sermons, but for

the locus of this hermeneutic in the imitation of Mary’s paradoxes—her speech as well as her

silence and her desire as well as her humility. The multivalent image of the garden was capacious

enough to encompass these multiple aspects of Marian love, as virgin, bride, and mother. As such,

In emphasizing the spiritual opportunities provided by the imitation of the Virgin Mary

CHAPTER FOUR Full of God: Mystical Union, Spiritual Birth, and Mary’s Consent in the Evangelical Pearl, the Temple of Our Soul, and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons

## Introduction

In the Catholic diocese of Cologne in the early 1530s, the Ave Maria was a familiar prayer.484

Mary was hailed enthusiastically and often, in communal devotion and in private petitions.485 It

was recited with particular defiance in Catholic regions since the prayer was a particular target of

early Lutheran Reformers.486 Readers of the Evangelical Pearl (printed 1535-6) however, would

have gained a new perspective on this prayer. In addition to greeting Mary, the author of the Pearl

exhorts her audience to be greeted as Mary. Having painstakingly walked her through the inner,

spiritual meaning of this prayer, the author addresses the reader directly, telling her: “O my soul,

if you wish to become always interior and virtuous and aware of your origin within you, so take

note and do after the perfect example and clear mirror of the Virgin Mary, how she was interiorly

and exteriorly.”487 The author of the Pearl unambiguously presents Mary as the model for a form

of interior, mystical life that can and should be accessed within the daily devotional expressions

of her audience. This is not an isolated incident in the Pearl. Indeed, Mary’s centrality is one of

the most consistent elements of this sprawling devotional compilation, and of two later texts that

The 162 Arnhem Mystical Sermons, like the Temple of Our Soul, explicitly presents a

Part 2. The Life of My Soul: Liturgy, Prayer, and Mystagogy

All three of these texts can be described as mystagogical, in that they instruct and guide

their audience in pursuit of the encounter with God. They share an insistent concern for cultivating

an elevated form of spiritual life among their readers. As the author of the Pearl writes in her

introduction, the book is a guide for those “spiritual people” [geestelike luyden] to whom Christ

spoke when he told the rich young man to leave all things behind and follow him naked. The

author writes “This little book treats this letting-go,” for those who climb above the virtues to the

contemplation and peace of “hanging” in God.538 The Temple’s directive to become the temple in

which Christ celebrates the liturgy is directed to “inward holy people” [inwendige heilige

menschen] and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons similarly exhort the “inner soul” [ynnige ziel] to

“receive God interiorly.”539 This occurs not through extraordinary actions, but within everyday

devotional activities, particularly prayer (in the Pearl) and the liturgy (in the Temple and the

Arnhem Mystical Sermons), which can be understood and practiced in a mystical way, and which

can stimulate an encounter with God expressed in the highest and most radical mystical terms.

In their explicit liturgical focus these three works return to early Christian understandings

of “mystagogy” as the interpretation of the mysteries of the sacraments.540 The liturgy, as a

The theme of the interiorization of the liturgy was developed in part through the reception

of Tauler, who was omnipresent in the spiritual milieu of the sixteenth-century Low Countries.559

Tauler’s sermons tended to focus more on the “global” thematic focus of various liturgical feasts,

rather than on the exegesis of individual liturgical readings or the specifics of their performance

context, making them a nimble and flexible resource, especially for educated, experienced, and

relatively autonomous communities of women.560 The texts were popular not necessarily for their

direct use in liturgical rites, but because they could help in “orienting” their audience into the spirit

and duties of each liturgical season, likely during refectory or chapter reading.561 Of particular

significance was Tauler’s account of the three births of Christ, and their parallels with key

moments in the Christmas liturgy, which was repurposed and reconfigured in the accounts of

spiritual birth in the Pearl, the Temple, and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons, as will be discussed in

depth below.562

This interiorization of the liturgy is, in a sense, already part of the liturgical encounter.

Jones writes that Tauler and Suso present the Divine Office, as “a form of spiritual training that

orders the ground of the soul so that it might receive divine experience.”577 As such, monastic

practices and the virtues they sought to inculcate are a means of facilitating the “self-divestment”

of the soul conveyed by mystical terms such as the Eckhartian gelâzenheit.578 In this way, instead

of stifling women’s affective spirituality and mysticism, adherence to the regulations of the

Reformed order could also be a vehicle for advancing spiritual or mystical ambitions.579

The Pearl’s attention to prayer and liturgy is equally enthusiastic, but, I would argue, even

more creative. The text valorizes prayer and liturgy, but its goal is not to teach its audience to

sublimate themselves along the grooves and grids of the liturgical framework, but to tunnel

curiously around its nooks and crannies, extracting its spiritual ore. While, in response to looming

Protestant destabilization, the text elevates the significance of these hallmarks of traditional

religion, it also untethers them from the loci of priest and place. With regard to both liturgy and

prayer, the book guides its reader through a twofold process of interiorization. The text reveals a

deeper meaning for everyday spiritual practices that can be accessed by ambitious spiritual strivers;

it also makes portable and internal these practices of prayer, enabling them to be accessed and

activated at any time, without being dependent on context, calendar, or preacher.

The Virgin Mary, I will argue, is another traditional “hook,” upon which the author of the

Pearl, the Temple, and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons hangs an array of interpretive associations

that simultaneously reinforce and dismantle theological foundations. It is her most archetypical

and recognizable aspects that provide opportunities for creative reinterpretation, but these attempts

## Conclusions

In the Pearl and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons, Mary’s consent is highlighted and emphasized

in the climactic account of spiritual birth, a process which is extended to the individual soul. We

have already seen in Chapter One Mary’s consent or fiat dramatically staged in Bernard’s IV

Homilies. These sixteenth-century texts make explicit, however, that which Bernard only

implies—that Mary’s consent is already preexistent. Indeed, they go far beyond this, to the extent

that Mary experiences all three births rather than only the historical birth. This is not necessarily a

total theological departure. Bernard and Eckhart both discuss Mary’s prevenient purification as

enabling her virginal conception. However, these texts show a much greater interest in how this

happened. They devote immense attention to questions of Mary’s freedom and consent. These

attributes are not framed in opposition to her pious virtues, but are instead developed through the

reading of her virtues as the perfection of her contemplative abilities.

This is not to say that these texts fully satisfy the question of how Mary’s consent can be both

free and preordained. But this is likely not a question that would have concerned their authors or

readers, for whom the imitation of Mary was the highest goal of spiritual life. In elevating Mary

as an example of mystical contemplation, these texts stress that the mystical encounter is possible,

for the human person, and specifically for devout women, to whom the invitation to imitate Mary

is continuously extended. This is sometimes figured through the erotic and agentic language we

have seen describing Mary’s virtues, particularly her humility, in these texts as well as in the texts

moral context, as when he writes in an extended metaphor of the Garden of Eden found in The Realm of Lovers that anyone whose faculties of higher reason consent to eat of the fruits (lust) offered by woman (the senses) will be exiled from paradise, that is, separated from God. Ruusbroec, Realm of Lovers, CCCM 103, p. 220. Similar expressions warning against the will’s consent to unchastity can be found in The Spiritual Tabernacle, The Twelve Beguines, and in a letter to Catherine of Leuven (Letter IV). There is one reference in Ruusbroec to consent in the context of Mary’s Annunciation. In the opening Prologue of the Spiritual Espousals, Ruusbroec presents the Annunciation as a wedding between Christ as the Bridegroom, Mary as the Bride, God the Father as the approving father-in-law and the Holy Spirit as the priest who blesses the marriage. When he writes that “the glorious Virgin gave that consent,” we can see this as a legible step in the establishment of this marriage as legitimate. The concept, however, is not especially relevant for Ruusbroec’s mysticism.

## CONCLUSION The Quest for Annunciations

The four chapters above have explored a wide range of mystical manifestations of Mary as

virgin, bride, and mother. In Sermon 138 of the Arnhem Mystical Sermons, however, another

superlative is added to Mary’s repertoire. In this sermon in honor of the feast of Mary’s purification

or Candlemas [lychtmysse dach] she is also presented as the “highest and first priest.”685Though

the image is not completely unprecedented, the presentation here, like so much of the imagery of

the Arnhem Mystical Sermons, is lively, detailed, and idiosyncratic.686

blessed virgin and mother of purity,” and especially as the highest example of detachment

[gelatenheit], obedience, and love. While Christ was commonly figured as the first priest, Sermon

I have argued that Mary was particularly central as a model in what I have called

mystagogical texts: sermons, visionary texts, liturgical commentaries and other works that instruct,

guide, and exhort their audience toward the mystical encounter. In thinking about how these works

describe, exhort, and in some cases enact this encounter through the figure of Mary, I have brought

say “I want nothing,” and to say “I want only God.”697 I might suggest then, that an even more

effective encapsulation of the paradox of mystical desire might be found in the ambivalent optative

of Mary’s fiat: let it be done. Certeau himself suggests this when he writes that mystical discourse,

the attempt to summon the missing body through language, might be described as a “quest for

‘annunciations,’ for words that take on body, for childbirth by the ear.”698 While Certeau writes

about the emergence of mystic discourse in the specific context of the hermeneutic and

confessional ruptures of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, his unnamed evocation of the

Virgin Mary nevertheless captures the desire described, exhorted, and evoked by these late

medieval texts for an encounter that transforms from the inside out.699

The figure of the Virgin Mary then, I have tried to convey throughout these pages does

not resolve, but rather underscores tensions of consent and agency that continually trouble both

Marian and mystical spirituality. Such questions of agency are particularly difficult to resolve for

those texts whose authors and audiences are so enigmatic or unknown—including the works of

Hadewijch, the Limburg Sermons, the Pearl, the Temple, and the Arnhem Mystical Sermons. Even

Bernard’s Homilies, with their contradictory and conflicting accounts of their audience and their

shifting modes of address, raise more questions than they answer. These texts’ own exploration of

Mary’s paradoxes, however, make a convincing argument for allowing these questions and

contradictions to linger, to create space for interpretation and imagination. These texts, after all,

present themselves as guides, not only to a specific historical audience, but to anyone willing to

be shaped according to Mary’s example—to all those willing to undertake her “quest for
